questions.question: Q1. Define electric potential and potential difference.
questions.answer: Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point: V = U/q. Potential difference ΔV between two points is the work per unit charge: ΔV = W/q. SI unit = volt (V) = J/C.
questions.example: A 9 V battery moves charge so each coulomb gains 9 J of energy.

questions.question: Q2. Find the potential due to a +3 μC charge at 0.1 m (k=9×10⁹).
Q3. Define the electron volt and its value in joules.
questions.answer: One electron volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V: 1 eV = e×1 V = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J. It is a unit of energy, not of potential.
questions.example: A 100 eV electron has kinetic energy 1.6×10⁻¹⁷ J.

questions.question: Q4. State the relation between potential and electric field for a uniform field.
questions.answer: Potential difference is related to field by ΔV = −∫E·dl; for a uniform field over distance d, ΔV = −Ed, so E = −dV/dx. The field points from high to low potential.
questions.example: A uniform 100 V/m field drops 20 V over 0.2 m.

questions.question: Q5. A 2 C charge is moved between points A (V=50 V) and B (V=20 V). Find the work done by the external agent.
questions.answer: W_external = q(V_B − V_A) = 2(20 − 50) = −60 J (the external agent does −60 J; the field does +60 J). ▥ 21.1 Potential, Potential Difference & Electron Volt  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Potential vs Potential Energy vs Potential Difference Electron Volt (eV) — Quick Reference ▣ 21.2–21.3 Equipotential & Potential Gradient
questions.example: The field does positive work moving + charge from high to low V.

questions.question: Q6. Define equipotential surfaces and state their properties.
questions.answer: An equipotential surface is a surface on which the potential is the same everywhere. Properties: no work is done moving a charge along it, the electric field is perpendicular to it, and equipotentials never cross.
questions.shortcut: E ⟂ equipotential ; no work on it.
questions.example: A charged conductor's surface is equipotential.

questions.question: Q7. Find the potential energy of two charges +q and −q separated by 0.2 m, q = 1 μC.
questions.answer: U = kq₁q₂/r = 9×10⁹×(1×10⁻⁶)(−1×10⁻⁶)/0.2 = −45×10⁻⁶ = −4.5×10⁻⁵ J (negative, attractive bound pair).
questions.example: −4.5×10⁻⁵ J; it takes that much to separate them.

questions.question: Q8. Explain potential gradient and its relation to electric field.
questions.answer: Potential gradient is the rate of change of potential with distance in the direction of the field: |dV/dx|. The electric field magnitude equals the negative potential gradient: E = −dV/dx (V decreases in the field direction).
questions.example: Between two 1 cm plates at 10 V: E = 10/0.01 = 1000 V/m.

questions.question: Q9. The potential of a charge distribution is V = kQ/r. Find the field from it.
questions.answer: E = −dV/dr = −d/dr(kQ/r) = kQ/r² (radial), the same as Coulomb's law (potential → field via gradient).
questions.example: Differentiate V = kQ/r to recover E = kQ/r².

questions.question: Q10. How does a charged conducting sphere distribute its charge and what is V at its centre?
questions.answer: Charge resides on the surface (uniform for a sphere); the potential is constant everywhere inside (equal to the surface value V = kQ/R) and E inside is zero. So the centre potential is kQ/R.
questions.example: A 1 m radius sphere with Q has V = kQ at the centre.

questions.question: Q11. Find the work to bring a +1 μC charge to the surface of a +2 μC sphere of radius 0.1 m from infinity.
questions.answer: W = qΔV = q(V − 0) = (1×10⁻⁶)(kQ/r) = (1×10⁻⁶)(9×10⁹×2×10⁻⁶/0.1) = 1×10⁻⁶×1.8×10⁵ = 0.18 J. ▥ 21.2–21.3 Equipotential & Potential Gradient  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Equipotential vs Field Lines Potential Gradient vs Field Intensity PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the potential of a point charge and of a set of charges.
theoryItems.answer: For a single charge, V = kq/r. For several charges, the potential is the algebraic sum (a scalar, so we add, not vector-add): V = Σkqᵢ/rᵢ. This is the key reason potential is often easier than the field.
theoryItems.example: Point charge at 0.1 m, q = 3 μC → 2.7×10⁵ V.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the relation E = −dV/dx for a uniform field.
theoryItems.answer: For a uniform field, moving a charge q a distance dx in the field direction does work −qE dx = q dV, so dV/dx = −E, i.e. E = −dV/dx (the field points from high to low potential). Magnitude |E| = |dV/dx|.
theoryItems.example: Two parallel plates 1 cm apart at 10 V: E = 1000 V/m.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. Define electric potential, potential difference and the electron volt.
theoryItems.answer: Potential V at a point = work per unit positive charge from infinity (J/C, volt). Potential difference ΔV = work per unit charge between two points. An electron volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron moving through 1 V: 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J.
theoryItems.shortcut: V = U/q ; ΔV = W/q ; 1 eV = 1.6e-19 J.
theoryItems.example: 9 V battery → each coulomb gains 9 J.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T4. Compare the electric field and the electric potential.
theoryItems.answer: The field E is a vector, the force per unit charge, and depends on the direction; the potential V is a scalar, the work per unit charge, and can be added algebraically. E = −∇V links them; V is easier for multiple charges (scalar sum).
theoryItems.shortcut: E: vector, force; V: scalar, energy. E = −∇V.
theoryItems.example: Add potentials as scalars; add fields as vectors.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain equipotential surfaces and their relation to the field.
theoryItems.answer: An equipotential surface is everywhere the same potential; no work is done moving a charge along it, and the electric field is perpendicular to it (E = −∇V). Equipotentials never cross; the spacing of lines reflects the field strength.
theoryItems.shortcut: E ⟂ equipotential ; no work on it ; never cross.
theoryItems.example: A charged conductor's surface is equipotential.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain potential energy of two charges and its sign.
theoryItems.answer: U = kq₁q₂/r. If the charges are like, U > 0 (work must be done to bring them together); if unlike, U < 0 (they attract, releasing energy as they approach). The negative value for opposite charges means a bound state.
theoryItems.example: An electron in an atom is a bound (negative U) state.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the potential of a charged conducting sphere and inside it.
theoryItems.answer: For a conducting sphere of radius R and charge Q, V = kQ/r outside (as if a point charge); inside the conductor, the potential is constant and equal to the surface value kQ/R (since E_inside = 0). This is why the surface is equipotential and the centre has the same potential.
theoryItems.shortcut: Outside V = kQ/r ; inside V = kQ/R (constant).
theoryItems.example: The potential inside a charged conductor is uniform.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain potential gradient and how a voltmeter measures it.
theoryItems.answer: The potential gradient is |dV/dx|, the potential change per unit distance, equal to the field magnitude. A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points; for a uniform field, E = V/d (field = gradient).
theoryItems.example: A probe voltmeter reads the potential difference.

theoryItems.question: [Viva] T9. Professor: 'If I bring two equal positive charges together, is the potential energy at infinity higher or lower? Why?'
theoryItems.answer: It is lower at a finite separation and higher at infinity: to separate two like charges, one must do work against their mutual repulsion, so the system's potential energy increases (U ∝ 1/r). At infinity U = 0; as they approach, U becomes positive and large.
theoryItems.shortcut: Like charges: U > 0, grows as they approach.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T10. A 2 C charge is moved from a point at 50 V to one at 20 V. Find the work done by the external agent and by the field.
theoryItems.answer: W_ext = q(V_B − V_A) = 2(20 − 50) = −60 J (external does −60 J); the field does +60 J (moves + charge from high to low potential, doing positive work).
theoryItems.example: The field does 60 J of work.

▣ 21.1 Potential, Potential Difference & Electron Volt
Q1. Define electric potential and potential difference.

Answer:  Electric potential V at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point: V = U/q. Potential difference ΔV between two points is the work per unit charge: ΔV = W/q. SI unit = volt (V) = J/C.
⚡ Shortcut:  V = U/q ; ΔV = W/q.
Example:  A 9 V battery moves charge so each coulomb gains 9 J of energy.
Q2. Find the potential due to a +3 μC charge at 0.1 m (k=9×10⁹).
⚡ Shortcut:  V = kq/r (scalar, add algebraically).
Example:  ≈ 270 kV.
Q3. Define the electron volt and its value in joules.
Answer:  One electron volt (eV) is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V: 1 eV = e×1 V = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J. It is a unit of energy, not of potential.
⚡ Shortcut:  1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J.
Example:  A 100 eV electron has kinetic energy 1.6×10⁻¹⁷ J.
Q4. State the relation between potential and electric field for a uniform field.
Answer:  Potential difference is related to field by ΔV = −∫E·dl; for a uniform field over distance d, ΔV = −Ed, so E = −dV/dx. The field points from high to low potential.
⚡ Shortcut:  E = −dV/dx ; E points high→low V.
Example:  A uniform 100 V/m field drops 20 V over 0.2 m.
Q5. A 2 C charge is moved between points A (V=50 V) and B (V=20 V). Find the work done by the external agent.
Answer:  W_external = q(V_B − V_A) = 2(20 − 50) = −60 J (the external agent does −60 J; the field does +60 J).
⚡ Shortcut:  W_ext = q(V_f − V_i).
Example:  The field does positive work moving + charge from high to low V.

▣ 21.2–21.3 Equipotential & Potential Gradient
Q6. Define equipotential surfaces and state their properties.

Answer:  An equipotential surface is a surface on which the potential is the same everywhere. Properties: no work is done moving a charge along it, the electric field is perpendicular to it, and equipotentials never cross.
⚡ Shortcut:  E ⟂ equipotential ; no work on it.
Example:  A charged conductor's surface is equipotential.
Q7. Find the potential energy of two charges +q and −q separated by 0.2 m, q = 1 μC.
Answer:  U = kq₁q₂/r = 9×10⁹×(1×10⁻⁶)(−1×10⁻⁶)/0.2 = −45×10⁻⁶ = −4.5×10⁻⁵ J (negative, attractive bound pair).
⚡ Shortcut:  U = kq₁q₂/r (sign matters).
Example:  −4.5×10⁻⁵ J; it takes that much to separate them.
Q8. Explain potential gradient and its relation to electric field.

Answer:  Potential gradient is the rate of change of potential with distance in the direction of the field: |dV/dx|. The electric field magnitude equals the negative potential gradient: E = −dV/dx (V decreases in the field direction).
⚡ Shortcut:  E = −dV/dx (magnitude = |dV/dx|).
Example:  Between two 1 cm plates at 10 V: E = 10/0.01 = 1000 V/m.
Q9. The potential of a charge distribution is V = kQ/r. Find the field from it.
Answer:  E = −dV/dr = −d/dr(kQ/r) = kQ/r² (radial), the same as Coulomb's law (potential → field via gradient).
⚡ Shortcut:  E = −dV/dr.
Example:  Differentiate V = kQ/r to recover E = kQ/r².
Q10. How does a charged conducting sphere distribute its charge and what is V at its centre?
Answer:  Charge resides on the surface (uniform for a sphere); the potential is constant everywhere inside (equal to the surface value V = kQ/R) and E inside is zero. So the centre potential is kQ/R.
⚡ Shortcut:  V_inside = V_surface = kQ/R ; E_inside = 0.
Example:  A 1 m radius sphere with Q has V = kQ at the centre.
Q11. Find the work to bring a +1 μC charge to the surface of a +2 μC sphere of radius 0.1 m from infinity.
⚡ Shortcut:  W = q(kQ/r).
Example:  0.18 J of work.
